subject: Career
title: Negotiating Your First Raise
description: A micro-lesson that makes Negotiating Your First Raise usable.

hook.text: You've been in the role for a year. You deserve a raise. But how do you ask without sounding greedy?

buildup.text: Raise negotiations require preparation: document your wins, research market rates, and choose your timing.

discovery.text: The best time to negotiate a raise is after a visible win — a completed project, positive review, or new responsibility.

twist.text: Most managers expect raise requests. It's not confrontational — it's professional. Not asking is the bigger mistake.

climax.text: Lead with value: 'Here's what I've contributed. Here's the market rate. I'd like to discuss alignment.'

punchline.text: Asking for a raise isn't greedy. Not knowing your value is costly.

quiz.question: When is the best time to negotiate a raise?
options: After a visible win like a completed project or positive review

details.summary: Your first raise negotiation sets the precedent for every future compensation conversation at the company. Timing it after a demonstrable achievement, preparing a value brief, and requesting a formal meeting all signal professional maturity and strategic thinking.
details.whyItMatters: Workers who negotiate their first raise within the first eighteen months earn significantly more over five years. The first raise conversation establishes your reputation as someone who advocates for fair compensation.
takeaways: Time your first raise request after a clear, measurable win
Prepare a one-page brief documenting your contributions
Set a formal meeting; do not negotiate casually in a hallway

faq.question: How soon after starting a new job should I negotiate my first raise?
faq.answer: Most professionals wait twelve to eighteen months, ideally timing the ask to coincide with a performance review cycle or a completed project milestone. Asking too soon without results can appear premature.

faq.question: What should I include in a value brief for my manager?
faq.answer: Document specific projects, revenue impact, cost savings, client wins, and any scope expansion beyond your original job description. Quantify results wherever possible and connect each achievement to team or company goals.
